description: Team Lixsin is Liya Ovalı, a 4th grade student from Turkey. We made "Forgotten Explorers: Moon Adventure", a story game for kids: you drive a little robot across the Moon and find 7 real NASA machines that are still there, like the Apollo 11 laser reflector and the Apollo 15 Lunar Rover. Each machine tells its own story and asks a quiz question for a star. We love the Moon, robots and storytelling!
summary: Forgotten Explorers: Moon Adventure is a story game for school-age space fans (ages 8–11). The player drives a small explorer robot across a map of the Moon and discovers 7 real pieces of NASA hardware that are still there today: the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage and laser reflector, the robot lander Surveyor 3, the Apollo 12 seismometer, the Apollo 15 Lunar Rover, Charlie Duke's family photo from Apollo 16 and the Apollo 17 Challenger descent stage. Each machine "comes back to life" and tells its own story in first person: what it is, why it was sent and what science it made possible, for example that the Apollo 11 laser reflector still shows the Moon moving about 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year. After each story, a quiz question (21 questions, picked at random each game) lets the player win a star, and finding all 7 machines earns the Moon Explorer badge. Instead of dense technical pages, kids learn through play and form a personal connection with these forgotten robotic explorers. The game is a single HTML file that runs offline on computers and tablets.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Forgotten Explorers: Moon Adventure is a browser game that tells the story of NASA hardware left on the Moon. The player names a little explorer robot and drives it across a Moon map with the arrow keys or touch buttons. A yellow arrow and a mini map lead to 7 real machines: Eagle (Apollo 11 descent stage), the Apollo 11 laser reflector, Surveyor 3, the Apollo 12 seismometer, the Apollo 15 Lunar Rover, Charlie Duke's family photo (Apollo 16) and Challenger (Apollo 17 descent stage).

HOW IT WORKS

When the robot reaches a machine, the machine talks in first person in a short, kid-friendly story: what it is, why it was sent, and what science it made possible (for example, moonquakes recorded by the seismometer, or the laser reflector that still measures the Earth–Moon distance today). Then a star question appears. There are 21 questions (3 per machine) and one is picked at random each game, with shuffled answers, so the game can be played again. Wrong answers can be retried. Finding all 7 machines earns the Moon Explorer badge.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Kids usually hear only about active missions. Our game turns dense historical facts into a story and a game, so 8–11 year olds learn about engineering and science by exploring, and feel a personal connection to these "forgotten" robotic explorers.

TOOLS

One self-contained HTML file with CSS and JavaScript (canvas). It runs offline in any modern browser, on computers and tablets. All graphics are drawn with code. Each machine is placed by the real latitude and longitude of its landing site (the map is not to scale).

CREATIVITY AND CONSIDERATIONS

The machines themselves are the storytellers. We focused on accuracy (facts checked against NASA sources), short sentences for young readers, no time pressure, and touch controls for tablets. The project was designed by a 4th grade student, made by a kid for kids.
